title: Over a field an injective matrix has a nonzero maximal minor
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], $n,p\ge0$ integers and $B$ a $p\times n$ matrix with entries in $K$ [def-weil-matrix] such that the $K$-linear map $K^n\to K^p$, $v\mapsto Bv$, is injective. Then $n\le p$, and there is a set $S=\{i_1<\dots<i_n\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,p\}$ of $n$ row indices such that the $n\times n$ submatrix $B_S=(b_{i_x j})_{1\le x,j\le n}$ of $B$ on the rows $S$ and all columns [def-weil-submatrix] has nonzero determinant [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], $\det B_S\neq0$ (for $n=0$, $S=\emptyset$ and $\det B_S=1$). Here $K^r$ is the set of $r$-tuples, with coordinatewise operations, and $(Bv)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}v_j$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00MY (lemma-exact-depth-zero-local, line 24678) for the field R = K (a field is a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal 0, and 0 = Ann(1) is an associated prime) applied to the complex 0 -> K^n -> K^p, with Lemma Tag 00MW (lemma-trivial-case-exact, line 24739) parts (1),(3) and Definition Tag 00MV (definition-rank, line 24722); tags verified in tags/tags: 00MY,algebra-lemma-exact-depth-zero-local; 00MW,algebra-lemma-trivial-case-exact; 00MV,algebra-definition-rank. Classical linear algebra (row rank equals column rank).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-injective-coordinate-linear-map-retraction] to $f(v)=Bv$. This is linear because finite sums distribute over addition and scalar multiplication, and is injective by hypothesis. Obtain a linear $g:K^p\to K^n$ with $g(Bv)=v$.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, lines 282-288; agent argument using a linear retraction, rather than the original 00MY/00MW route

proof.text: Let $e_i\in K^p$ denote the tuple with $1$ in position $i$ and $0$ elsewhere, and define an $n\times p$ matrix $C$ by $c_{ji}=g(e_i)_j$ [def-weil-matrix]. For any $w\in K^p$, $w=\sum_iw_ie_i$, so linearity gives $g(w)_j=\sum_iw_ic_{ji}=(Cw)_j$. Apply this to $w=B\epsilon_k$, where $\epsilon_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit tuple of $K^n$. Then $\sum_i c_{ji}b_{ik}=g(B\epsilon_k)_j=(\epsilon_k)_j=\delta_{jk}$. Thus $CB=I_n$. This also holds for $n=0$, when there are no entries to check.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, lines 282-288; agent argument using a linear retraction, rather than the original 00MY/00MW route

proof.text: By [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], $\det I_n=1$: only the identity permutation contributes to its Leibniz sum (also for $n=0$, by the empty product convention). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] to $C$ of size $n\times p$ and $B$ of size $p\times n$: $$1=\det(CB)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\},\ |S|=n}\det(C^S)\det(B_S).$$ Here $C^S$ has the columns indexed by $S$ and $B_S$ the rows indexed by $S$, in increasing order, exactly as in the cited statement; Cauchy–Binet does not require $n\le p$.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, lines 282-288; agent argument using a linear retraction, rather than the original 00MY/00MW route

proof.text: If every $\det(B_S)$ in the finite sum were zero, each summand would be zero and the sum would be zero, contrary to $1\ne0$ in the field [def-weil-field]. Thus at least one subset $S$ of size $n$ has $\det(B_S)\ne0$. Since it is a subset of the $p$ row indices, $n=|S|\le p$. Writing its elements in increasing order produces exactly the submatrix [def-weil-submatrix] in the conclusion. If $n=0$, this is $S=\emptyset$ and its determinant is $1$ by [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant].
